facts.statement: The genus is named Alamosaurus.
facts.quote: taxon: Alamosaurus

facts.statement: Alamosaurus was described by Gilmore in 1922.
facts.quote: authority: Gilmore, 1922

facts.statement: The type species of the genus is Alamosaurus sanjuanensis.
facts.quote: type_species: Alamosaurus sanjuanensis

facts.statement: Alamosaurus is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs meaning "Ojo Alamo lizard".
facts.quote: Alamosaurus (; meaning "Ojo Alamo lizard") is a genus of titanosaurian sauropod dinosaurs

facts.statement: Alamosaurus lived in southwestern North America during the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period.
facts.quote: from the Maastrichtian age of the Late Cretaceous period in what is now southwestern North America

facts.statement: Alamosaurus is one of the few sauropods known to have lived in North America following a 30-million-year gap in the fossil record.
facts.quote: It is one of the only known sauropods to have inhabited North America after the nearly 30-million-year absence of sauropods from the continent's fossil record

facts.statement: Some specimens suggest that Alamosaurus may have been larger than the standard estimates.
facts.quote: though some specimens indicate a larger body size

facts.statement: The holotype of Alamosaurus was discovered in June 1921 in New Mexico by Gilmore, Reeside, and Sternberg.
facts.quote: The holotype was discovered in June 1921 by Charles Whitney Gilmore, John Bernard Reeside, and Charles Hazelius Sternberg at the Barrel Springs Arroyo in the Naashoibito Member of the Ojo Alamo Formation (or Kirtland Formation under a different definition) of New Mexico

facts.statement: Gilmore described the holotype (a left scapula) and paratype (a right ischium) in 1922.
facts.quote: Smithsonian paleontologist Gilmore originally described holotype USNM 10486, a left scapula (shoulder bone), and the paratype USNM 10487, a right ischium (pelvic bone) in 1922

facts.statement: Gilmore posthumously described specimen USNM 15560 in 1946, which was found in Utah in 1937.
facts.quote: In 1946, Gilmore posthumously described a more complete specimen, USNM 15560, found on June 15, 1937, on the North Horn Mountain of Utah by George B. Pearce

facts.statement: In 2025, Gregory S. Paul reclassified USNM 15560 as the holotype of the new species Utetitan zellaguymondeweyae.
facts.quote: In 2025, Gregory S. Paul assigned USNM 15560 as the holotype of the new taxon Utetitan zellaguymondeweyae

facts.statement: Fossils of an unknown titanosaur related to Alamosaurus have been found in northeastern Chihuahua, Mexico.
facts.quote: Fossils of an unknown titanosaur closely related to Alamosaurus have been collected from northeastern Chihuahua, Mexico

facts.statement: Although no skull has been found, rod-shaped teeth associated with Alamosaurus skeletons likely belonged to the animal.
facts.quote: Though no skull has ever been found, rod-shaped teeth have been found with Alamosaurus skeletons and probably belonged to this dinosaur

facts.statement: Alamosaurus uniquely possessed pneumatised ribs extending for two-thirds of their length among titanosaurs.
facts.quote: Uniquely among titanosaurs, the ribs of Alamosaurus are pneumatised for two-thirds of the rib length

facts.statement: Trackways indicate Alamosaurus walked slowly at speeds between 3.2 and 4 km/h without dragging its tail.
facts.quote: Trackways show that Alamosaurus walked slowly at speeds of 3.2 – 4 km/h without dragging their tails

facts.statement: Thomas Holtz hypothesized that the maximum length could be 30 meters or more and weight 72.5 to 80 tonnes.
facts.quote: Thomas Holtz proposed a maximum length of around 30 m or more and an approximate weight of 72.5–80 tonnes (80–88 short tons) or more

facts.statement: Scott Hartman estimates Alamosaurus at 28-30 meters based on a tibia, but notes scientists are unsure if that tibia belongs to Alamosaurus or a new species.
facts.quote: Scott Hartman estimates Alamosaurus, based on a huge incomplete tibia that probably refers to it, being slightly shorter at 28 - 30 m and equal in weight to other massive titanosaurs, such as Argentinosaurus and Puertasaurus, though he states that scientists do not know whether the massive tibia belongs to an Alamosaurus or a completely new species of sauropod

facts.statement: It is debated whether fossils from formations like the North Horn, Black Peaks, and Javelina belong to Alamosaurus or a distinct genus.
facts.quote: Fossils recovered from other Maastrichtian formations have also been referred to Alamosaurus, like the North Horn Formation of Utah, the Black Peaks and the Javelina Formations of Texas, though these specimens may represent a distinct genus

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene classified Alamosaurus within the family Titanosauridae in 1927.
facts.quote: In 1927, Friedrich von Huene placed it in Titanosauridae.

facts.statement: Some phylogenetic analyses place Alamosaurus in the subgroup Opisthocoelicaudiinae within the family Saltasauridae, uniting it with Opisthocoelicaudia.
facts.quote: One major analysis unites Alamosaurus with Opisthocoelicaudia in the subgroup Opisthocoelicaudiinae of Saltasauridae.

facts.statement: A competing analysis identifies Alamosaurus as a sister taxon to Pellegrinisaurus, placing both genera outside the family Saltasauridae.
facts.quote: A major competing analysis finds Alamosaurus as a sister taxon to Pellegrinisaurus, with both genera located just outside Saltasauridae.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses have recovered Alamosaurus in varying positions, including as an opisthocoelicaudiine, a saltasaurine, or entirely outside Saltasauridae.
facts.quote: The position of Alamosaurus recovered by phylogenetic analyses varies.

facts.statement: Alamosaurus fossils are notably found in the Naashoibito Member of the Ojo Alamo Formation, dated to approximately 66.87 million and 66.38 million years ago.
facts.quote: Alamosaurus fossils are most notably found in the Naashoibito Member of the Ojo Alamo Formation (or Kirtland Formation), dated to 66.87 ± 0.04 Ma and 66.38 ± 0.08 Ma around 5 metres (16 ft) and 3.5 metres (11 ft) above the base of the member respectively.

facts.statement: Thomas M. Lehman describes the Late Cretaceous fauna in southern North America, dominated by Alamosaurus and Quetzalcoatlus, as representing semi-arid inland plains with a superficially 'Jurassic' aspect.
facts.quote: In the south of Late Cretaceous North America, the transition from the Edmontonian to the Lancian faunal stages is even more dramatic than it was in the north. Thomas M. Lehman describes it as "the abrupt reemergence of a fauna with a superficially 'Jurassic' aspect. These faunas are dominated by Alamosaurus and feature abundant Quetzalcoatlus in Texas. The Alamosaurus-Quetzalcoatlus association probably represent semi-arid inland plains.

facts.statement: Fossils of Alamosaurus found in the Evanston Formation in Wyoming indicate it shared its environment with Triceratops.
facts.quote: Fossils of Alamosaurus unearthed in the Evanston Formation in Wyoming indicate it shared its environment with Triceratops.

facts.statement: The 'austral immigrant' hypothesis, suggesting Alamosaurus descended from South American titanosaurs, is challenged by the possibility that Maastrichtian routes between continents consisted of separate islands hindering dispersal.
facts.quote: The austral immigrant hypothesis has been challenged on the grounds that the routes connecting North and South America during the Maastrichtian may have consisted of separate islands, which would have presented challenges to the dispersal of titanosaurs.

facts.statement: The 'inland herbivore' scenario suggests titanosaurs were present in North America throughout the Late Cretaceous but were rarely preserved in upland environments they favored, rather than being truly absent.
facts.quote: A second scenario, termed the "inland herbivore" scenario, suggests that titanosaurs were present in North America throughout the Late Cretaceous and that their apparent absence reflects the relative rarity of fossil sites preserving the upland environments that titanosaurs favored, rather than their true absence from the continent.

facts.statement: A third hypothesis proposes that Alamosaurus originated in Asia rather than South America, despite many dinosaurs crossing between the continents via the Bering land bridge.
facts.quote: A third option is that, as in the austral immigrant scenario, Alamosaurus is not native to North America, but originated in Asia instead of South America.

facts.statement: It is debated whether an Asian origin is viable because sauropods were poorly adapted for the high-latitude, inhospitable environment of Beringia.
facts.quote: Though many dinosaurs crossed between Asia and North America across the Bering land bridge, sauropods were poorly adapted for high-latitude environments and Beringia would have been an inhospitable environment for titanosaurs.

facts.statement: While origins are debated, several studies favor a South American origin, with Chiarenza et al. (2022) regarding it as the only viable origin for Alamosaurus.
facts.quote: Overall, a South American origin has been favored by several studies and Chiarenza et al. (2022) regarded it as "the only viable origin" for Alamosaurus.

facts.statement: Definitive specimens of Alamosaurus sanjuanensis come from the Ojo Alamo Formation.
facts.quote: Definitive specimens of Alamosaurus sanjuanensis are known from the Ojo Alamo Formation.

facts.statement: Specimens previously attributed to Alamosaurus from the North Horn, Black Peaks, and Javelina Formations were reassigned to the genus Utetitan in 2025.
facts.quote: Previously referred specimens from the North Horn Formation, the Black Peaks Formation and possibly the Javelina Formation have been assigned to Utetitan in 2025.

facts.statement: Alamosaurus lived during the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Cretácico superior

facts.statement: Alamosaurus lived approximately 70 to 66 million years ago during the Late Maastrichtian stage of the Late Cretaceous in what is now North America.
facts.quote: que vivió a finales del período Cretácico, hace aproximadamente 70 y 66 millones de años, a fines del Maastrichtiense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The genus Alamosaurus was named by Gilmore in 1922.
facts.quote: genus_authority: Gilmore, 1922

facts.statement: The species Alamosaurus sanjuanensis was named by Gilmore in 1922.
facts.quote: species_authority: Gilmore, 1922

facts.statement: Alamosaurus is the only described North American titanosaur from the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Es el único titanosauriano norteamericano descrito de finales del Cretácico

facts.statement: Adult Alamosaurus are estimated to have been about 26 meters long, 5 meters high at the shoulders, and weighed up to 30 to 35 tonnes.
facts.quote: Los adultos habrían medido alrededor de 26 metros de largo, 5 metros de alto hasta los hombros y pesaron hasta 30-35 toneladas

facts.statement: Alamosaurus had a small head supported by a long, robust neck, a broad and sturdy torso, cylindrical legs for weight support, and a relatively slender tail for balance and locomotion coordination.
facts.quote: Como saurópodo, tenía una cabeza pequeña, sostenida por un largo y robusto cuello, con un torso amplio y corpulento, patas cilíndricas para soportar su peso y una cola, relativamente esbelta, para ayudarle en el equilibrio y coordinación locomotora.

facts.statement: Alamosaurus generally resembled Brachiosaurus more than Diplodocus.
facts.quote: Su aspecto general llegaría a recordar más a Brachiosaurus que a Diplodocus.

facts.statement: Alamosaurus was a giant quadrupedal herbivore with long necks and tails and relatively long legs.
facts.quote: Alamosaurus fue un herbívoro cuadrúpedo gigante con un cuello y colas largos y patas relativamente también largas.

facts.statement: Although no skull has been found, stick-shaped teeth associated with Alamosaurus skeletons likely belong to this dinosaur.
facts.quote: Aunque ningún cráneo ha sido encontrado, los dientes en forma de bastoncillos se han encontrado asociados a esqueletos de Alamosaurus y probablemente pertenecía a este dinosaurio.

facts.statement: The presence of osteoderms distributed along the back of Alamosaurus has been recently confirmed, serving as defensive armor against predators.
facts.quote: la presencia de osteodermos fueron confirmados en este género recientemente, estructura orgánica distribuida a lo largo y ancho del dorso del animal, muy útil como armadura defensiva ante el ataque de depredadores.

facts.statement: Scientists have not yet agreed on whether a massive tibia found in the region belongs to Alamosaurus or to a completely new sauropod species.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, por el momento, los científicos no se han puesto de acuerdo si la masiva tibia pertenece a un Alamosaurus o una especie completamente nueva de saurópodo.

facts.statement: Scott Hartman estimates Alamosaurus was 28 to 30 meters long and weighed as much as massive titanosaurs like Argentinosaurus and Puertasaurus, but notes uncertainty regarding the origin of the massive tibia used for this estimate.
facts.quote: Scott Hartman estima que Alamosaurus, basándose en una enorme tibia incompleta que probablemente se refiere a este, es ligeramente más corto, de 28 a 30 metros, e igual en peso a otros titanosaurios masivos, como Argentinosaurus y Puertasaurus, aunque afirma que los científicos no saben si la enorme tibia pertenece a un Alamosaurus o a una especie completamente nueva de saurópodo.

facts.statement: The holotype USNM 10486 was discovered in June 1921 in the Kirtland Formation of New Mexico by Charles Whitney Gilmore, John Bernard Reeside, and Charles Hazelius Sternberg.
facts.quote: El holotipo, USNM 10486, fue descubierto en la Formación Kirtland de Nuevo México en junio de 1921 por Charles Whitney Gilmore , John Bernard Reeside y Charles Hazelius Sternberg

facts.statement: Remains of Alamosaurus have been discovered throughout the North American southwest.
facts.quote: Los restos de Alamosaurus se han descubierto por todo el sudoeste norteamericano

facts.statement: Alamosaurus fossils have been found in Maastrichtian formations including the North Horn Formation in Utah and the Picos Negros, El Picacho, and Javelina Formations in Texas.
facts.quote: Huesos de Alamosaurus ha sido encontrado en otras formaciones del Maastrichtiano, como en la Formación North Horn de Utah y en la Formación Picos Negros, Formación El Picacho y Formación Javelina de Texas

facts.statement: In 1946, a more complete skeleton was found in Utah consisting of a complete tail, a complete right forelimb except for the foot tip, and both ischia.
facts.quote: En 1946, encontró un esqueleto más completo en Utah, consistiendo en una cola completa, un miembro anterior derecho completo excepto por el extremo del pie y ambos isquiones

facts.statement: The most complete known specimen is a recently discovered juvenile skeleton in Texas that allowed for accurate estimates of length and mass.
facts.quote: El espécimen más completo conocido es un esqueleto juvenil recientemente descubierto en Texas, que permitió estimaciones correctas de la longitud y masa

facts.statement: In 2015, it was confirmed that a previously described specimen included osteoderms, marking the first confirmation of their presence in Alamosaurus.
facts.quote: En 2015 se mostró que este espécimen, el cual ya había sido descrito, también incluía osteodermos, la primera confirmación de que estos estaban presentes en Alamosaurus

facts.statement: Alamosaurus belongs to the parent group Saltasaurinae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Saltasaurinae

facts.statement: Alamosaurus is classified in the family Saltasauridae.
facts.quote: Family: Saltasauridae

facts.statement: Alamosaurus is classified in the class Saurischia.
facts.quote: Class: Saurischia

facts.statement: The time range for Alamosaurus is from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian, spanning from 83.6 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Campanian to Maastrichtian (83.6 to 66 million years ago)
